title: For engineers & builders
problem: You keep meeting the same failure modes — the late project, the creeping complexity, the metric that gets gamed. They already have names.
blurb: The laws you learn the hard way, gathered in one place. Ship dates, systems that grow to fit their org chart, quirks that become contracts — the patterns every engineer eventually runs into, explained and sourced.

title: For product & decision-makers
problem: Every call you make runs on incomplete information and a mind full of shortcuts. Knowing the shortcuts by name is how you stop them steering you.
blurb: The traps that bend judgement — targets that get gamed, plans that always run long, the sunk cost you can't walk away from — and the biases that skew a decision before you've made it. Learn the shape, catch yourself mid-mistake.

title: For writers & communicators
problem: Getting an idea from your head into someone else's is a fight against noise, refutation, and the curse of already knowing the answer.
blurb: The laws of attention, clarity, and persuasion — why most of everything is mediocre, why a headline that asks a question can be answered “no”, and why the fastest way to a right answer is to post a wrong one. Tools for anyone who writes to be read.

title: For leaders & managers
problem: Organisations have their own physics. People rise to where they stall, work expands to fill the calendar, and the structure you build quietly shapes what you can build.
blurb: The laws of organisations and incentives — competence promoted past its limit, bureaucracies that grow whatever you do, and the diffusion of responsibility that leaves everyone waiting on everyone else. For anyone trying to get a group to do good work.

title: For curious minds
problem: You want sharper tools for thinking — ways to weigh a claim, remember what you read, and notice when your own mind is fooling you.
blurb: Razors for cutting through nonsense, the effects that shape what you remember, and the biases that quietly distort what you believe. A starter kit for thinking more clearly about everything else.

title: For designers & interface builders
problem: Every argument about a layout is really an argument about attention, memory and time — and those have been measured. The findings have names.
blurb: The laws behind the decisions you defend in reviews. How long a target takes to hit, how long a list takes to choose from, how much a person can hold in their head at once, and which part of an experience they will actually remember afterwards — each one measured, sourced, and honest about where it stops applying.

title: For teachers & learners
problem: Almost everything that makes learning stick feels worse in the moment than the thing that doesn't. That is not an opinion; it is a set of findings with names.
blurb: Why cramming loses to spacing, why testing yourself beats rereading, why knowing a subject makes you worse at explaining it, and why the least skilled are the least able to see it. The evidence behind teaching practice, rated for how well established each finding actually is.

title: For negotiators & dealmakers
problem: The number that gets said first moves the number you end up with. So does the order of the asks, and so does what each side stands to lose rather than gain.
blurb: What is actually known about how people bargain: the pull of the first figure on the table, the obligation a small favour creates, why an identical deal reads differently as a loss than as a gain, and why winning an auction is evidence you overpaid. Sourced findings, with the replication record where it matters.

title: For investors & markets
problem: Most of the ways a portfolio goes wrong are named, documented and older than you are — and almost none of them feel like mistakes at the time.
blurb: The market's recurring shapes: why a run of good judgement is usually a run of good luck about to end, why the quiet part of a boom is when the risk is built, why the seller always knows more than the buyer, and why the sample you are learning from is the one that survived. Rated honestly — several of these are contested, and the entries say so.

title: For researchers & analysts
problem: A result can be real, significant and completely misleading. The ways that happens have names, and most of them are older than the software you found them with.
blurb: The failure modes of evidence: an association that reverses when you split the data, an extreme reading that was always going to drift back, a target that stops measuring the thing once you manage against it, and a hypothesis drawn around the shots after they landed. What to check before believing your own chart.
